RESUMO

Introdução:

A

hospitalização

pediátrica

pode

impactar

o

comportamento

alimentar

infantil

e

a

dinâmica

alimentar

familiar

pois

representa

um

evento

potencialmente

estressor,

associado

a

alterações

na

rotina,

exposição

a

procedimentos

invasivos

e

impacto

emocional

para

crianças

e

seus

cuidadores.

Nesse

contexto,

as

dificuldades

alimentares

pediátricas

(DAPs)

constituem

uma

condição

frequente,

com

potencial

impacto

no

estado

nutricional,

no

crescimento

e

no

desenvolvimento

infantil.

Os

estilos

parentais

de

alimentação

emergem,

nesse

sentido,

como

um

elemento

central

para

a

compreensão

das

práticas

alimentares

e

das

respostas

da

criança

frente

à

alimentação.

Eles

influenciam

o

desenvolvimento

dos

comportamentos

alimentares,

contudo,

a

relação

entre

essas

práticas

e

as

DAPs

ainda

é

pouco

explorada

no

cenário

da

hospitalização

pediátrica.

O

objetivo

do

estudo

foi

analisar

os

estilos

parentais

de

alimentação

e

sua

associação

com

DAPs

em

crianças

hospitalizadas.

Metodologia:

Trata-se

de

um

estudo

transversal

realizado

com

crianças

de

seis

meses

a

14

anos

incompletos

hospitalizadas

na

unidade

de

internação

pediátrica

do

Hospital

de

Clínicas

de

Porto

Alegre

e

seus

cuidadores

primários.

Foram

excluídas

crianças

em

uso

exclusivo

de

via

alimentar

alternativa

ou

com

ingestão

oral

apenas

para

estímulo.

Os

dados

foram

coletados

por

meio

de

prontuário

eletrônico

das

crianças

e

entrevistas

estruturadas

para

os

cuidadores.

Os

estilos

parentais

de

alimentação

foram

avaliados

pelo

Questionário

de

Estilos

Parentais

na

Alimentação

(QEPA),

considerando

tanto

os

pontos

de

corte

propostos

no

estudo

original

quanto

a

média

da

própria

amostra

para

a

classificação

das

dimensões

de

exigência

e

responsividade.

As

DAPs

foram

identificadas

por

meio

da

Escala

Brasileira

de

Alimentação

Infantil

(EBAI)

e

do

critério

funcional

do

American

Speech-Language-Hearing

Association

National

Outcome

Measurement

System

(ASHA-NOMS).

Os

dados

foram

analisados

por

estatística

descritiva

e

testes

qui-quadrado

de

Pearson

e

análise

de

variância,

adotando-se

nível

de

significância

de

5%.

Resultados:

Foram

analisadas

337

pares

de

cuidador-criança.

Observou-se

predominância

do

sexo

masculino

entre

as

crianças

(56,7%),

com

mediana

de

idade

de

4

anos

(2-7).

73,3%

delas

apresentavam

hospitalizações

prévias

e

52,5%

foram

classificadas

com

Condições

Crônicas

Complexas

(CCC).

Entre

os

cuidadores,

88,1%

eram

do

sexo

feminino

e

43,9%

apresentavam

insegurança

alimentar.

As

DAPs

estavam

presentes

em

25,5%

das

crianças.

A

utilização

de

diferentes

pontos

de

corte

resultou

em

variações

na

distribuição

dos

estilos

parentais,

com

frequência

de

alta

responsividade

de

85,2%

pelo

ponto

de

corte

original

e

52,5%

pela

média

da

amostra

(p<0,001),

enquanto

a

alta

exigência

variou

de

30%

para

46%

(p<0,001).

O

estilo

indulgente

foi

o

mais

frequente,

variando

de

37,1%

para

61,4%

conforme

o

critério

adotado.

Verificou-se

associação

entre

maior

exigência

parental

e

presença

de

DAPs

(p=0,018),

percepção

de

DAPs

(p=0,004),

dificuldades

na

aceitação

alimentar

e

resistência

a

novos

alimentos

(p<0,001),

além

de

problemas

na

progressão

de

texturas

(p=0,020).

A

menor

responsividade

associou-se

à

percepção

de

DAPs

(p=0,013),

dificuldades

na

aceitação

alimentar

(p=0,015)

e

resistência

a

novos

alimentos

(p=0,017).

Conclusão:

Os

estilos

parentais

de

alimentação

estão

associados

às

DAPs

em

crianças

hospitalizadas,

destacando-se

o

papel

da

maior

exigência

e

menor

responsividade

como

fatores

relacionados

a

piores

desfechos

alimentares.

Além

disso,

a

escolha

dos

pontos

de

corte

influencia

significativamente

a

classificação

dos

estilos

parentais.

ABSTRACT

Introduction:

Pediatric

hospitalization

may

impact

children’s

eating

behavior

and

family

feeding

dynamics,

as

it

represents

a

potentially

stressful

event

associated

with

changes

in

routine,

exposure

to

invasive

procedures,

and

emotional

burden

for

children

and

their

caregivers.

In

this

context,

Pediatric

Feeding

Disorder

(PFD)

is

a

frequent

condition

with

potential

consequences

for

nutritional

status,

growth,

and

child

development.

Feeding

parenting

styles

emerge

as

a

central

element

for

understanding

feeding

practices

and

children’s

responses

to

food.

These

styles

influence

the

development

of

eating

behaviors;

however,

the

relationship

between

these

practices

and

PFD

remains

underexplored

in

the

pediatric

hospitalization

setting.

The

purpose

of

study

is

to

analyze

feeding

parenting

styles

and

their

association

with

PFD

in

hospitalized

children.

Methods:

This

was

a

cross-sectional

study

conducted

with

children

aged

six

months

to

under

14

years

hospitalized

in

the

pediatric

inpatient

unit

of

Hospital

de

Clínicas

de

Porto

Alegre

and

their

primary

caregivers.

Children

exclusively

receiving

alternative

feeding

routes

or

with

oral

intake

only

for

stimulation

were

excluded.

Data

were

collected

from

children’s

electronic

medical

records

and

structured

caregiver

interviews.

Feeding

parenting

styles

were

assessed

using

the

Caregiver’s

Feeding

Styles

Questionnaire

(CFSQ),

considering

both

the

cut-off

points

proposed

in

the

original

study

and

the

sample

mean

to

classify

the

dimensions

of

demandingness

and

responsiveness.

PFD

was

identified

using

the

Montreal

Children’s

Hospital

Feeding

Scale

(MCH-FS)

and

the

functional

criteria

of

the

American

Speech-Language-Hearing

Association

National

Outcome

Measurement

System

(ASHA-NOMS).

Data

were

analyzed

using

descriptive

statistics,

Pearson’s

chi-square

tests,

and

analysis

of

variance,

adopting

a

significance

level

of

5%.

Results:

A

total

of

337

caregiver–child

dyads

were

analyzed.

Most

children

were

male

(56.7%),

with

a

median

age

of

4

years

(IQR

2–7).

Previous

hospitalizations

were

reported

in

73.3%

of

cases,

and

52.5%

of

children

were

classified

as

having

Complex

Chronic

Conditions

(CCC).

Among

caregivers,

88.1%

were

female,

and

43.9%

experienced

food

insecurity.

PFD

was

identified

in

25.5%

of

children.

The

use

of

different

cut-off

points

resulted

in

variations

in

the

distribution

of

feeding

parenting

styles,

with

high

responsiveness

observed

in

85.2%

using

the

original

cut-off

and

52.5%

using

the

sample

mean

(p<0.001),

while

high

demandingness

ranged

from

30%

to

46%

(p<0.001).

The

indulgent

style

was

the

most

frequent,

ranging

from

37.1%

to

61.4%

depending

on

the

adopted

criterion.

Higher

parental

demandingness

was

associated

with

the

presence

of

PFD

(p=0.018),

caregiver

perception

of

PFD

(p=0.004),

feeding

acceptance

difficulties

and

resistance

to

new

foods

(p<0.001),

and

problems

with

texture

progression

(p=0.020).

Lower

responsiveness

was

associated

with

caregiver

perception

of

PFD

(p=0.013),

feeding

acceptance

difficulties

(p=0.015),

and

resistance

to

new

foods

(p=0.017).

Conclusion:

Feeding

parenting

styles

are

associated

with

PFD

in

hospitalized

children,

highlighting

the

role

of

higher

demandingness

and

lower

responsiveness

as

factors

related

to

poorer

feeding

outcomes.

Additionally,

the

choice

of

cut-off

points

significantly

influences

the

classification

of

feeding

parenting

styles.

and

Disorders

ABSTRACT

Introduction:

Pediatric

hospitalization

may

impact

children’s

eating

behavior

and

family

feeding

dynamics,

as

it

represents

a

potentially

stressful

event

associated

with

changes

in

routine,

exposure

to

invasive

procedures,

and

emotional

burden

for

children

and

their

caregivers.

In

this

context,

Pediatric

Feeding

Disorder

(PFD)

is

a

frequent

condition

with

potential

consequences

for

nutritional

status,

growth,

and

child

development.

Feeding

parenting

styles

emerge

as

a

central

element

for

understanding

feeding

practices

and

children’s

responses

to

food.

These

styles

influence

the

development

of

eating

behaviors;

however,

the

relationship

between

these

practices

and

PFD

remains

underexplored

in

the

pediatric

hospitalization

setting.

The

purpose

of

study

is

to

analyze

feeding

parenting

styles

and

their

association

with

PFD

in

hospitalized

children.

Methods:

This

was

a

cross-sectional

study

conducted

with

children

aged

six

months

to

under

14

years

hospitalized

in

the

pediatric

inpatient

unit

of

Hospital

de

Clínicas

de

Porto

Alegre

and

their

primary

caregivers.

Children

exclusively

receiving

alternative

feeding

routes

or

with

oral

intake

only

for

stimulation

were

excluded.

Data

were

collected

from

children’s

electronic

medical

records

and

structured

caregiver

interviews.

Feeding

parenting

styles

were

assessed

using

the

Caregiver’s

Feeding

Styles

Questionnaire

(CFSQ),

considering

both

the

cut-off

points

proposed

in

the

original

study

and

the

sample

mean

to

classify

the

dimensions

of

demandingness

and

responsiveness.

PFD

was

identified

using

the

Montreal

Children’s

Hospital

Feeding

Scale

(MCH-FS)

and

the

functional

criteria

of

the

American

Speech-Language-Hearing

Association

National

Outcome

Measurement

System

(ASHA-NOMS).

Data

were

analyzed

using

descriptive

statistics,

Pearson’s

chi-square

tests,

and

analysis

of

variance,

adopting

a

significance

level

of

5%.

Results:

A

total

of

337

caregiver–child

dyads

were

analyzed.

Most

children

were

male

(56.7%),

with

a

median

age

of

4

years

(IQR

2–7).

Previous

hospitalizations

were

reported

in

73.3%

of

cases,

and

52.5%

of

children

were

classified

as

having

Complex

Chronic

Conditions

(CCC).

Among

caregivers,

88.1%

were

female,

and

43.9%

experienced

food

insecurity.

PFD

was

identified

in

25.5%

of

children.

The

use

of

different

cut-off

points

resulted

in

variations

in

the

distribution

of

feeding

parenting

styles,

with

high

responsiveness

observed

in

85.2%

using

the

original

cut-off

and

52.5%

using

the

sample

mean

(p<0.001),

while

high

demandingness

ranged

from

30%

to

46%

(p<0.001).

The

indulgent

style

was

the

most

frequent,

ranging

from

37.1%

to

61.4%

depending

on

the

adopted

criterion.

Higher

parental

demandingness

was

associated

with

the

presence

of

PFD

(p=0.018),

caregiver

perception

of

PFD

(p=0.004),

feeding

acceptance

difficulties

and

resistance

to

new

foods

(p<0.001),

and

problems

with

texture

progression

(p=0.020).

Lower

responsiveness

was

associated

with

caregiver

perception

of

PFD

(p=0.013),

feeding

acceptance

difficulties

(p=0.015),

and

resistance

to

new

foods

(p=0.017).

Conclusion:

Feeding

parenting

styles

are

associated

with

PFD

in

hospitalized

children,

highlighting

the

role

of

higher

demandingness

and

lower

responsiveness

as

factors

related

to

poorer

feeding

outcomes.

Additionally,

the

choice

of

cut-off

points

significantly

influences

the

classification

of

feeding

parenting

styles.

and

Eating

Disorders

of

Childhood;

Child,

Hospitalized.
